speaker: Chelsea Finn
title: No Priors Ep. 107 | With Physical Intelligence Co-Founder Chelsea Finn
question: In robotics, how far can observational videos of humans take you when training robot control models?
guest: I think the data can have a lot of value, but by itself it won't get you very far. There are some really nice analogies you can make: for example, if you watch an Olympic swimmer swim a race, even if you had their strength, their practice at moving their own muscles to accomplish what they're accomplishing is essential for being able to do it. Or if you're trying to learn how to hit a tennis ball well, you won't be able to learn it just by watching the pros. Now, maybe these examples seem a little contrived because they're talking about experts. The reason why I make those analogies is that we humans are experts at low-level motor control already for a variety of things, and our robots are not. I think the robots actually need the experience from their own body in order to learn. So it's really promising to leverage that form of data, especially to expand on the robot's own experience, but it's really going to be essential to actually have the data from the robot itself too.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Quite far, but not all the way. Human video is the only robot-relevant data source at internet scale, and it has proven valuable for learning what transfers across embodiments: visual representations (R3M, VIP), affordances and object-interaction priors, task structure, reward or value functions, and world or video-prediction models. Approaches like latent-action pretraining (LAPA, Genie-style models, NVIDIA's GR00T) and egocentric data collection (EgoMimic, Tesla's and Figure's human-video efforts) show that pretraining on human footage substantially improves sample efficiency and generalization to new objects, scenes and tasks.

The limits are structural. Videos contain no action labels, no forces or tactile signals, and humans have different bodies, so the embodiment gap in kinematics and contact dynamics must be bridged somehow. In practice, the best results still need some robot data, whether teleoperation, simulation, or on-robot reinforcement learning, to ground the learned priors in actual motor commands, especially for dexterous, contact-rich manipulation.

So the honest summary: human video can supply most of the "what to do" and a growing share of "how", reducing robot data needs by perhaps an order of magnitude, but zero-shot, video-only control remains limited to relatively simple skills.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Observational human videos can carry most of the perceptual, semantic, and kinematic burden of robot learning, but they cannot take you all the way to general-purpose low-level control alone. At scale, human videos teach visual representations, world dynamics, object affordances, task planning, and latent action priors, cutting the expensive robot teleoperation data needed by orders of magnitude. Using 3D hand-pose retargeting, point tracks, or visual embodiment editing, recent systems even achieve zero-shot transfer from egocentric human clips to robots on quasi-static tasks like pick-and-place and pouring. Yet passive video hits a hard ceiling at the embodiment and modality gap. Pixels do not capture joint torques, grip forces, tactile slip, friction, or proprioception, and human anatomy maps imperfectly onto robot kinematics and actuators. For contact-rich, force-sensitive, or dynamically unstable skills—like tight insertion or forceful tool use—closing the last mile still requires grounded on-robot interaction through teleoperated fine-tuning or reinforcement learning.

noweb.answer:
Observational videos of humans can take robot learning remarkably far on perception, planning, and sample efficiency, yet fall short of producing complete, zero-shot controllers on their own. At scale, human videos teach models rich visual representations, object affordances, task semantics, and intuitive physics—such as how objects move and interact when manipulated. Using latent action models, 3D hand-pose tracking, or predictive world models, researchers can extract coarse motion priors that slash the amount of expensive robot teleoperation data needed for downstream tasks by orders of magnitude.

However, human video hits a hard ceiling at low-level actuation due to missing action labels and the embodiment gap. Pixels record neither motor torques nor the proprioceptive and tactile forces essential for contact-rich tasks like tight assembly or grasping fragile objects, and human hands differ sharply in kinematics and compliance from robot hardware. Ultimately, human videos build a strong foundation for *what* to do and *where* to move, but grounded on-robot demonstrations or reinforcement learning remain indispensable for the final mile of reliable physical execution.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Human videos can take you surprisingly far, but not all the way. Watching people gives a robot useful priors: visual representations (R3M, VIP, MVP), knowledge of affordances and object interactions, predictive world models, and "latent actions" learned without labels (LAPA, Genie-style models, NVIDIA's GR00T N1). Egocentric datasets with hand tracking, such as Ego4D, EgoMimic and Apple's EgoDex, can be retargeted into motion or point-track targets that policies then imitate. Physical Intelligence has reported that human-to-robot transfer gets stronger as vision-language-action models are pretrained at larger scale.

The ceiling comes from what video doesn't capture. It has no action labels, forces, torques or tactile feedback. Human bodies and hands also differ from robot arms and grippers in reach, joints and dynamics, so contact-heavy, precise or forceful manipulation needs information that pixels don't provide.

So the current consensus is that human video works best for pretraining, cutting how much robot data you need and improving generalization to new objects and scenes. You still need some teleoperated or on-robot data, plus reinforcement learning or other fine-tuning, to ground behavior in the specific body and get it reliable. Video sets the "what" and roughly the "how"; robot data supplies the precise physical "how."

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Observational human videos can take you far on high-level understanding, but they cannot deliver reliable low-level robot control on their own. Because everyday video is abundant and diverse, it excels at pretraining visual representations, object affordances, task structure, and predictive world models, teaching a robot what to do and how a scene should evolve. Paired with latent action modeling or hand-pose retargeting, human video substantially improves generalization and reduces the amount of robot data needed.

However, passive video hits a hard ceiling at physical execution. It is inherently action-free, showing visual outcomes without the joint commands, contact forces, torques, or tactile feedback required for dexterous manipulation. It also suffers from a stark embodiment gap between human anatomy and robotic hardware, and rarely captures closed-loop error recovery. In practice, human video serves best as a scalable pretraining or co-training foundation, while robot teleoperation, simulation, or real-world reinforcement learning remains essential to ground those priors into executable control.

noweb.answer:
Observational videos of humans can take robot control models surprisingly far on perception, semantics, and high-level planning, but they rarely suffice for end-to-end physical execution on their own. Because human video is abundant and diverse, it excels at pretraining visual representations, world models, and latent motion priors, teaching robots what objects afford, how multi-step tasks unfold, and roughly what trajectories achieve a goal. This dramatically improves generalization and reduces how much robot-specific data is needed downstream.

However, passive video hits a clear ceiling when translating intent into precise control. Videos lack explicit action labels, proprioception, and tactile or force feedback, making contact-rich manipulation difficult to learn from observation alone. They also create an embodiment gap: human hands, kinematics, and viewpoints differ substantially from most robotic hardware, and passive footage rarely shows how to recover from physical errors or disturbances. In practice, human video provides a powerful foundation, while reliable closed-loop control still requires grounding through robot teleoperation, simulation, or direct real-world interaction.

Human videos can teach a robot what a successful task looks like, which objects to interact with, and how those objects should move. For some manipulation tasks, that’s enough to train a policy that runs on a real robot without collecting robot demonstrations. Phantom and HumanEgo show this by extracting hand and object motion from video and translating it into actions the target robot can execute. [Phantom](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v305/lepert25a.html) · [HumanEgo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24934)

The main limit is that video shows motion, while control also depends on what caused it. A clip rarely reveals how hard someone squeezed, what they felt at contact, or which commands would produce the same result on a robot with a different gripper and range of motion. For precise, contact-heavy tasks or recovery when something goes wrong, robot demonstrations, simulation, or practice on the hardware can supply the missing feedback.

noweb.answer:
Human videos can teach robots a great deal about what to do and in what order. They show which objects matter, how people approach and manipulate them, and what success looks like. Models can use those cues to learn visual representations, predict useful intermediate goals, or infer motions that can be adapted to a robot. This can substantially reduce the amount of robot-specific training data needed.

The limit is that video rarely tells you exactly what command a robot should send. A person’s hand differs from a robot gripper, and ordinary footage leaves depth, contact forces, and hidden motions ambiguous. Video alone can sometimes support simple tasks when the motion is easy to infer and the robot already has suitable skills. For precise or contact-rich tasks, reliable execution usually requires grounding in the target robot through demonstrations, interaction, simulation, or an existing controller. Human video can teach the strategy at scale, while robot experience teaches how to carry it out.

Videos of people can teach a robot what success looks like and how a task usually unfolds. Watching someone open a drawer, for example, can help a model learn where to grasp, which way to pull, and when the drawer is open far enough. If the robot already knows how to reach, grasp, and pull, that information may be enough to apply those skills to a new drawer.

The harder step is turning visible motion into reliable control. A video rarely reveals how much force the person used or how they felt the handle begin to slip. A robot with a different gripper must also produce that motion using its own joints. Human videos can therefore reduce the robot demonstrations needed to learn a task. For reliable contact-rich manipulation, models generally still need some way to connect what they see to what the robot can do, such as robot action data, simulation, or feedback from practice.
